episodes.211861: An incoming shortwave trough brought showers and some thunderstorms to west Texas and southeast New Mexico overnight April 30th and especially during the morning of May 1st. During the morning of the 1st, rainfall became locally heavy at times, which resulting in flash flooding in urban and low-lying areas. Showers largely cleared the area during the afternoon of the 1st as the shortwave moved east of MAF's CWA, taking the best lift and moisture with it.

episodes.212742: On May 1, 2026, severe weather developed across South Texas as a shortwave trough moved eastward out of northern Mexico and interacted with a quasi-stationary frontal boundary draped across South Texas and the middle Texas coast. North of the front, a very moist air mass characterized by dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s combined with moderate instability to support widespread showers and thunderstorms. As the upper-level disturbance approached, increasing large-scale ascent and strengthening mid-level winds enhanced deep-layer shear, allowing some storms to become better organized and rotate. Despite extensive cloud cover and ongoing convection, sufficient instability remained in place for stronger updrafts capable of producing large hail. The combination of strengthening shear and organized storm structures also supported isolated severe wind gusts. Additionally, the development of a surface low along the Texas coast locally enhanced low-level wind fields and directional shear near the frontal boundary, creating a favorable environment for a brief, isolated tornado.

episodes.213855: Early May flooding in Southern Illinois occurred on the western and eastern borders. On the border with Missouri, well above normal April rainfall upstream along the Mississippi River from East Central Missouri and Central Illinois to Iowa/Wisconsin resulted in river levels on the Mississippi River rising into minor flood at Cape Girardeau to end April, with Thebes also observing minor flooding in early May. To the east, torrential training showers and thunderstorms along the White River basin on the 27th of April, including a zone of 3-5 inches, resulted in river levels rising into minor flood downstream on the Wabash River in early May at Mount Carmel and New Harmony. For both areas, impacts were mainly limited to bottomland agricultural areas and a few rural roads.
episodes.213856: Torrential training showers and thunderstorms along the White River basin on the 27th of April, including a zone of 3-5 inches, resulted in river levels rising into minor flood at Petersburg and Hazleton by the end of April, with minor flooding continuing into May. Minor flooding occurred downstream on the Wabash River in early May at Mount Carmel and New Harmony. Additional heavy rainfall on May 5th along the White River basin resulted in a secondary crest on the lower White River before river levels finally fell below flood stage mid-May. Impacts were limited to bottomland agricultural areas and oil wells, along with some rural roads.
episodes.213857: Well above normal April rainfall upstream along the Mississippi River from East Central Missouri and Central Illinois to Iowa/Wisconsin resulted in river levels on the Mississippi River rising into minor flood from Chester to Cape Girardeau to end April, with those two gages and Thebes observing minor flooding in early May. Impacts were limited to bottomland agricultural areas.

episodes.214310: Historic flooding from April 2026 continued into the month of May, most noteworthily in Cheboygan and Emmet counties, though conditions were improving overall, as the Pellston Regional Airport was finally able to partially reopen to commercial air traffic, and the alert status for the Cheboygan Dam was also finally lifted during this month.

Flooding impacts across Cheboygan county continued into the month of May, though on a downtrend. The Cheboygan Dam complex and areas downstream were removed from the Ready, Set, Go alert model on May 1st, and the Cheboygan River continued to trend down to more normal levels, as measured by a temporary gauge installed at the Lincoln Ave Bridge immediately upstream of the dam complex... falling below an initial level of 594.50ft above mean sea level by May 13th, and generally trending back toward somewhat more normal levels through the remainder of the month, save for an uptick around the second or third week of the month with some rainfall that briefly brought levels back up to 594.50ft MSL again. Additionally, crews working at the Alverno Dam were demobilized on May 1.

Flooding impacts continued into May for Emmet county, though improvements were had. The Pellston Regional Airport, KPLN, finally returned to service with one runway by May 5th, and to full operations by June 1.

Late April minor flooding continued through the middle of May along the White River near Petersburg, with river levels cresting several feet above flood stage on the 1st. After lowering towards the end of the first week of May, a secondary surge of water raised river levels slightly for the second week of May with a secondary crest May 12th. Impacts were mainly limited to low-lying agricultural lands and low oil fields, with portions of several county roads flooded.

The Rock River in the Fort Atkinson area continued to have impacts from high water. The floodwaters affected some park land and boat launchees, and partially flooded the following roads: Sinissippi Drive, Bark River Road from Kutz Road to Rock River Road and E Milwaukee Ave, and Rock River Rd from Highway 106 to the Fort Atkinson city limits.

The Rock River at Lake Koshkonong continued to have impacts from high water. Floodwaters reached Oxbow Bend Road in the area of the gauge on the east side of the lake. The following roads were flooded: the end of Road 9, end of Road 8 St, end of E Road 7, Lakeview Dr, Charley Bluff Rd north of Royce Dallman Park, parts of Lamp Rd, Willow Rd, parts of Blackhawk Island Rd. Water surrounded some structures on Lamp Rd and toward the end of Blackhawk Island Rd. Low lying areas of Lakeland Campground and Altpeter County Park flooded. There was water into yards along High Ridge Rd. Homes and docks in the Blackhawk Island area on the north side of Lake Koshkonong were affected by floodwaters.

Evidence of a high-end EF-1 (110mph) tornado was found in south- central Victoria County. Drone footage showed a scour track that began over farmland between Crouch Rd and HWY-185, and ended near Crouch Rd east of York Rd along with a track of debris. In between, several manufactured homes on Jared Rd, Lexie Ln, and York Rd suffered significant roof damage, broken windows, and scattered debris correlated to circulation of a tornado. One manufactured home was completely destroyed along Jared Rd. The tornado track was found to be around 1.1 miles long and a width of around 400 yards, spanning from 2:02-2:06pm CDT.
